structure.title: Essays 1–3 · What would an interpretation change?
structure.text: Kuypers begins with the problem of giving gravity a place in a quantum world. Violaris then brings the reader down to a cup of coffee to ask how much the entropy assigned to a system depends on the observer. Her next essay turns to what an experiment could settle between interpretations of quantum mechanics.

structure.title: Essays 4–7 · What could count as a witness?
structure.text: The discussion moves between locality, living systems and gravity. Several contributors share a practical difficulty. The thing a physicist wants to study can be extraordinarily hard to examine directly. How much could be inferred by measuring what happens to two other systems that interact through it?

structure.title: Essays 8–13 · What survives a change of theory?
structure.text: The later essays take up elegance, time, probability, entanglement and the status of effective theories. A dispute about what probability means in a branching universe sits beside a proposal about what heat measurements can reveal. The closing essay returns to gravity by asking how much physics can do with relations between bodies.

people.name: Maria Violaris
people.role: Author of the coffee and Copenhagen essays
people.text: A cup gives Violaris something ordinary enough for a reader to keep track of while she changes what an observer knows or can do. Her note about writing the essays also restores something the finished argument can hide, namely the particular disagreement that made the question worth pursuing.

people.name: Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral
people.text: Their essay describes physical systems in terms of which operations on information the laws permit. This lets them compare quantum physics and general relativity in a shared vocabulary. Whether that resemblance can help produce a theory of quantum gravity is a further question they explicitly raise.

context.title: An experimental witness
context.text: A witness is a measurable sign from which a physicist can infer something that is difficult to inspect directly. The inference needs assumptions. When an author proposes a witness, the crucial passage often explains why a system lacking the proposed property could not have produced the measured effect.

context.title: Several authors can use an equation and disagree
context.text: A physical theory may guide a calculation with extraordinary precision while leaving room for disputes about the entities that make its predictions come true. The contributors pursue different answers. An assertion in one essay can serve as a premise, an open question or a target of criticism in another.

passages.quote: they resist unification into a single, comprehensive framework.

notice.text: Date the laboratory scene in Weber's opening.
notice.why: It takes place in an imagined future. Details that make the reader feel present at an experiment can also make it easy to remember a proposed result as an observed one. Weber spends much of the essay explaining the distance between that morning and a working experiment.

passages.quote: Imagine a day in the future, in an old, musty physics lab

notice.text: Follow what the person with the coffee is allowed to change.
notice.why: Two observers may know different things about a cup. They may also have different instruments or be able to perform different operations. Keeping those differences apart gives the disagreement about entropy something concrete to turn on.

opening: Physics can predict an experiment exquisitely while leaving physicists arguing about what exists. The contributors to this collection take those arguments seriously: how quantum theory relates to gravity, what probability means, and whether apparently distant events require mysterious connections. These are researchers explaining problems they work on, including proposals that remain open to dispute. Reading across the essays brings the unsettled foundations into view, where getting the calculations right does not remove the need to say what kind of world could produce them.
